en: The Mahāyāna Sūtra titled *Āryabuddhabalādhānaprātihāryavikurvāṇanirdeśa*. Thus have I heard:
at one time the Blessed One was seated on the bank of the great river Nairañjanā together with the noble Avalokiteśvara.

He was honored, revered, and worshipped by seven thousand bodhisattvas led by Vajrapāṇi, Maitreya, and Mañjuśrī; by all the great śrāvakas led by Subhūti, Śāriputra, and Maudgalyāyana; and by all the Śakras, Brahmās, world-protectors, kings, ministers, brahmins, and householders.
Having finished his meal, the Blessed One sat down in the circle of the assembly and gladdened, incited, inspired, and delighted them with a discourse connected with the Dharma.
Then the Tathāgata, having gone from the city of Maharddhi to Vārāṇasī, sat down in the Āmrapālī grove within that circle of the assembly.
At that time, the great earth trembled and shook violently.

There stood a single great lion throne made of various jewels and fashioned from the seven precious substances; it was one yojana in height and half a yojana in width, comfortably arranged, exceedingly delightful, charming, and spread with divine cloths.
It was hung with various divine flowers and fruits, and possessed divine fragrance and color.
Beholding the roots of merit planted by the Tathāgatas, all sentient beings attained the patient acceptance of the non-arising of phenomena (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*).
Then, while seated upon the lion throne, the Blessed One attained the samādhi named *Buddhāvataṃsaka*.
Thereupon, arising from that samādhi, he addressed the Bodhisattva Noble Avalokiteśvara and Vajrapāṇi as follows:

O Avalokiteśvara, having gone to the great world-system and throughout the world-systems in the ten directions, you and Vajrapāṇi— both of you possessing great supernatural power— [should act] for the sake of those beings to be trained who are possessed of degenerations, lacking faith, of evil conduct, shrouded by afflictions, not knowing their mothers, not knowing their fathers, not honoring śramaṇas, not honoring brahmins, and who have no faith in the Three Jewels; for all of them, you two...
"Having attained the power of samādhi, condense and bring together [the teachings] within this garland of maṇḍalas.
Then, having heard the words of the Tathāgata, the noble Avalokiteśvara and Vajrapāṇi looked upon all sentient beings and entered the samādhi called "Inspiration.
By the power of that samādhi, the great earth shook, trembled, and quaked in six ways.
Within the trichiliocosm, from the Brahma world up to the realm of form, the manifestation of light from their two bodies occurred.
Then, from that radiance, these verses of exhortation issued forth.
At that time, at the conclusion of the verses issued from the light of their bodies, every single being in the trichiliocosm was informed and inspired by word of mouth.
All those beings, having abandoned wrong views, became endowed with right view. Those who were possessed of pride, intoxication, and arrogance became free from pride, intoxication, and arrogance.

Those who followed sensual desires and were heedless turned away from the eight unwholesome dharmas—such as taking life, taking what is not given, sexual misconduct, and so forth—and were established upon the Noble Eightfold Path.

Having abandoned all their restlessness, laughter, dancing, play, greed, anger, envy, passion, and so forth, they all became desirous of beholding, serving, attending upon, and hearing the Dharma from the Tathāgata. The Tathāgata was honored by gods, nāgas, yakṣas, gandharvas, asuras, kinnaras, garuḍas, mahoragas, kings, ministers, monks, nuns, laymen, and laywomen with divine flowers, garlands, perfumes, powders, robes, parasols, banners, flags, and other such offerings.

Then they all approached the Āmrapālī grove in the great city of Vārāṇasī, and by the power of the merit and roots of virtue planted under the Tathāgatas, they rained down a shower of flowers upon the Tathāgata. At that time, the Blessed One established the Āmrapālī grove in Jambudvīpa as extending for hundreds of thousands of millions of *yojanas* in every direction—
level like the palm of a hand, divine, delightful, and endowed with exquisite color.

It was adorned with celestial flower trees, fragrance trees, fruit trees, great jewel trees, wish-fulfilling trees (*kalpavṛkṣa*), clothing trees, and so forth; it was furnished with divine couches and thrones, radiant with strings of jeweled bands, yellow in hue, and graced by the sound of celestial tinkling bells,
just like the world-system of Sukhāvatī.
Thus, [the assembly] remained amidst a multitude that was pleasing, gladdening, lovely, and delightful—
filled with all the bodhisattvas, śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, devas, nāgas, yakṣas, gandharvas, asuras, garuḍas, kinnaras, mahoragas, laymen, laywomen, kings, ministers, brahmins, and householders.
Then the noble Bodhisattva Avalokiteśvara and Vajrapāṇi arose from their meditative absorption and approached the place where the Blessed One was.
Having approached and circumambulated the Blessed One three times to the right, he said this to the Blessed One:
"Blessed One, the Tathāgatas possess skillful means for the sake of maturing sentient beings.
Blessed One, there are many bodhisattvas, great śrāvakas, and kings of gods, nāgas, yakṣas, gandharvas, asuras, garuḍas, kinnaras, and mahoragas, as well as ministers, householders, and others."
The monks, nuns, laymen, and laywomen assembled through the splendor of the Tathāgata’s majesty and supernatural power.
"Excellent, excellent, noble sons!

It is even so, O sons of the Conqueror; such is the skillful means of the Tathāgatas for the sake of maturing sentient beings—according to their inclinations, according to how they have acquired roots of merit suitable for discipline, and according to the various dispositions of sentient beings."
Having understood their conduct, they teach the Dharma:
some beings are to be disciplined by Bodhisattvas, some by Śrāvakas, some by Pratyekabuddhas,
some by gods, some by Śakras, some by Brahmās, some by Nāgas, and some by those of great supernatural power.
Some are to be converted by means of a king; some by means of meditative concentration (*samādhi*); some by means of hearing the Dharma; some by means of miracles (*prātihārya*);

some by means of the Tathāgata’s final nirvāṇa; some by means of relics (*dhātu*); some are eager for conversion through the roots of merit arising from the construction of shrines, the entering [of monasteries], the building of monasteries, walking-paths, and gardens; and some are to be converted through the roots of merit arising from the commissioning of stone images, paintings, and images made of gold, silver, or bronze.

Some are to be converted by being eager for the roots of merit arising from honoring and revering the community of monks; some are to be converted by being eager for the roots of merit arising from inquiring about, writing, reciting, and honoring the sūtras; and some are eager for lamps, flowers, incense, perfumes, garlands, food, and ornaments.
They are not endowed with the dharmas of the roots of merit that pertain to the ultimate truth, nor are they endowed with the dharmas of nirvāṇa.
Moreover, O sons of the Conqueror, regarding all phenomena, there is nothing for the Tathāgatas that is unknown, unseen, unheard, or unperceived.
They know what has come to pass, and they know what is yet to come.
He knows little, or he knows much;
he knows the past.
He knows the present;
he knows the modes of conduct of all sentient beings;
he knows their course of action.
He knows the element;
he knows arising;
he knows rebirth.

It is just as, O sons of the Conqueror, a well-trained physician who has mastered the entire eightfold Ayurveda and is devoted to the application of all medicinal substances and instruments with skill regarding the elements, knows the constitution and knows the strength of sentient beings whose bodies are afflicted by various diseases.
He knows the time;
he knows the medicine;
[he knows it as] pertaining to wind, bile, phlegm, or a combination of all three.

He knows blood disorders, those born of undigested matter (*āmaja*), abdominal tumors (*gulma*), dropsy (*jalodara*), heart disease, leprosy, itching, ringworm, pustules, and the like, as well as poisons, erysipelas, and so forth.

Having understood all these, he applies various medicinal substances through the application of emetics, purgatives, powder-formulations, nasal therapies (*nasya*), vein-binding, and the application of ghee, oil, and hair-powders; by means of such methods for digestion and evacuation, he pacifies all those diseases of all sentient beings.
They shall be liberated from various diseases and from the fears of various diseases.

In the same way, O sons of the Conqueror, the Tathāgata—endowed with various samādhis, bases of psychic power, powers, fearlessnesses, the divine eye, the divine ear, and so forth, and possessed of the eightfold Āyurveda;

skilled in the application of the various elements and dispositions—is [the physician] for those afflicted by the diseases of the afflictions and secondary afflictions, such as the diseases of passion, hatred, and delusion.

For the sake of liberating beings who are intoxicated by pride and arrogance, and those shrouded by desire, grief, fear, and anger— liberating them from the realms of hell, the animal kingdom, and the world of Yama—

he liberates beings through various skillful means, various types of yogas, and various playful displays of meditative concentrations and supernatural powers. He establishes them in unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment and leads them to final nirvana in the realm of nirvana without remainder.

He will be completely liberated from unwholesome states and establishes them upon the noble eightfold path. Sons of good family, it is just as the orb of the moon, endowed with skill in means, manifests its own disappearance for the sake of those beings who are to be trained by roots of goodness according to their respective dispositions.
He displays the shape of a half-moon mandala; he displays the dark fortnights and the bright fortnights;
he displays the full moon mandala.
It dispels all blinding darkness and refreshes all grasses, forests, shrubs, medicinal herbs, fruits, and so forth.

In the same way, O sons of the Victorious One, the skill in the practice of the path of the Tathāgatas demonstrates parinirvāṇa for sentient beings shrouded by various sufferings and for sentient beings to be disciplined through various dispositions.
He displays his birth; he displays the sovereignty of a universal monarch (cakravartin);
he displays play, delight, women, laughter, dance, perfumes, garlands, and the pleasures of amorous sport.

He demonstrates the renunciation of the household life, the going forth into homelessness, and the practice of austerities; he demonstrates the subduing of Māra’s forces and the turning of the wheel of Dharma; and finally, he demonstrates the satisfaction of all sentient beings by raining down the great cloud of Dharma.

Even though the Tathāgatas have entered final nirvāṇa, they liberate all sentient beings simply through the performance of various offerings to the elements, the construction of stūpas, monasteries, and images, the going forth into homelessness, the renunciation of the world, the honoring of the community of monks, and the writing, reciting, and reading of the Vinaya and Dharma.
They liberate all sentient beings by means of those skilled in the methods of undertaking training, observance, vows, restraints, fasts, and moral discipline.

(From *Buddhabalādhānaprātihārya-sūtra* 181) They cause [beings] to rejoice, delivering them from all the hells, the animal realm, the world of Yama, the inopportune births, the states of woe, and the miserable destinies;
and by means of hearing the Dharma, they establish them in unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment.
Then, at that time, this thought occurred to certain sons of the gods of limited intelligence:
Thinking, "Does this Tathāgata wish to enter the realm of parinirvāṇa so soon?", they became dejected.
... For this purpose, he describes and indicates his parinirvāṇa;
having assembled a great assembly, he displays various miraculous transformations of supernatural power (*ṛddhi-vikurvāṇa-prātihārya*).
Just as the former Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksambuddhas performed the work of a Tathāgata by sustaining a very long life-span,
thereby liberating all sentient beings from birth, old age, sickness, death, sorrow, lamentation, pain, dejection, and despair.
Thinking, "In this way, this Tathāgata has not yet completed all the deeds of a Tathāgata;
therefore, he praises the transcendence of sorrow," they became silent.
Then Mañjuśrī Kumārabhūta, knowing the thoughts of those sons of gods with his own mind, addressed those sons of gods as follows:
Sons of gods, do not think thus; do not speak thus; do not be despondent in mind.

The Tathāgatas teach the Dharma to sentient beings of various dispositions by means of many skillful means—the power of their roots of merit, vows, and various wisdoms, meditative concentrations, and so forth.
O sons of gods, just as I have witnessed the skillful means of former Tathāgatas and their miraculous displays of supernatural power, so do I know this:
it is not that the Tathāgata desires to reveal or to further elaborate upon the great king of sūtras called the "Miracle of the Empowerment of the Buddha's Strength.
Moreover, O sons of gods, Tathāgatas do not pass into final nirvāṇa.
The parinirvāṇa of the Tathāgatas does not exist;
there is no exhaustion of their lifespan.
For immeasurable millions of koṭīs of kalpas, and for ineffable kalpas, the Tathāgatas remain.
Moreover, through skillful means, they manifest the final nirvana of sentient beings;
yet no coming or going exists for the Tathāgatas.
They manifest the disappearance of the true Dharma.

In whatever way he perceives sentient beings who are to be disciplined by means of final nirvāṇa, or disciplined according to their elements, or belonging to a degenerate age, and who thus fall into a lack of faith and a failure to honor or serve the Tathāgata— in that very way the Tathāgata manifests final nirvāṇa; yet, no passing away or transition whatsoever exists for the Tathāgatas.
All sentient beings have their roots of virtue fully ripened;
they long for a vision of the Tathāgata, are worthy of making offerings, and desire to hear the Dharma.
Just as the lunar disk shines, so too do the Tathāgatas arise in the world for the benefit of many people and for the happiness of many people.

"O sons of good family, as long as there is illumination and manifestation for gods and humans through the Three Jewels, yet no birth of the Tathāgatas exists— just as, for example, various forms are seen in a well-polished mirror-surface, but the object of sight does not exist therein, nor is any coming or going of the reflection seen— even so, O sons of the gods, the body of the Tathāgata is to be viewed."

Sons of good family, it is just as if a well-trained illusionist were to display various cities, gateways, and gardens, various chariots, the forms of universal monarchs, and various pleasures and games, and then make them vanish; yet no departure, arrival, or exit of those [illusions] is seen.
In the very same way, the appearance and final nirvana of the Tathāgatas are to be viewed.

Moreover, O sons of the gods, by virtue of their former vows, the Tathāgatas— even though they have entered final nirvāṇa, or have been in final nirvāṇa for an eon, or have been in final nirvāṇa for ten million eons— liberate sentient beings from all hells, animal births, the world of Yama, the unfavorable conditions, and the miserable destinies, and from all sufferings, even while residing in various world-systems, through the honoring and revering [of them], the construction of relic-stūpas and images, the taking up of their names, and the upholding and honoring of the True Dharma; and eventually, they lead them to fully awaken to unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment.

What need is there to mention those who will worship the Tathāgatas with direct offerings of perfumes, flowers, garlands, ointments, garments, and ornaments? And as for those sons of gods or any beings whatsoever who, having joined their palms in reverence, shall even once utter the name, saying "Homage to the Buddha," and cast a flower into the air; [their merit shall be immeasurable].

They shall all bring an end to suffering. Let alone flowers in the sky— whatever beings, training themselves for the sake of honoring the Tathāgata, shall uphold even a single precept of the Tathāgata for a single day,
a single night, or a single muhūrta, being intent upon the thought of worshipping the Tathāgata, they shall bring an end to all suffering.
Having practiced in successive stages, they will fully awaken to unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment.

And those who, for the sake of honoring the Tathāgata—even if it be only by scattering sand or performing acts of laughter, dance, childish play, or amusement—all of them, having brought an end to suffering, will fully awaken to unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment; what need is there to mention [those who do so with greater devotion]?

Those who, having fashioned a reliquary stūpa or an image containing relics, being supremely compassionate toward all sentient beings and having generated the mind set on unexcelled perfect enlightenment with the thought, "I shall liberate all sentient beings from sufferings," worship and display them with divine flowers, perfumes, garlands, ointments, powders, musical instruments, umbrellas, banners, and flags— they shall be liberated from the sufferings and the exhaustion of birth, old age, and death.
